daisypilotFind0.7<- gl.filter.callrate(daisypilot,method = "ind",threshold = 0.7)

pc <- gl.pcoa(daisypilotFind0.7, nfactors = 5)
gl.pcoa.plot(pc,daisypilotFind0.7,xaxis = 1,yaxis = 2)

It showed me following error, and I can't understand.

Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE) : arguments imply differing number of rows: 26, 0

Could I get some help from you about understanding and figuring out these? Thank you for taking time read this, and the dartR is a useful and resourceful tool, I hope I can use it more wisely.

Yunjia

messages.subject: Generate reduced gl object with fixed differences only
messages.subject_clean: Generate reduced gl object with fixed differences only
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I have a dataset of approx 5000 loci for a suspected hybrid zone and 2 putative parent species. I've run the fixed difference function to determine the number of fixed loci between the two parents and I'd like to now run a new hybrids analysis using only those loci.

My question is, how can I create a new genlight object that reduces my 5000 loci down to just the loci with fixed differences? I've explored both functions but I can't find a way to output a reduced genlight object and I'm afraid my R skills aren't quite up to the task of writing my own script (although I may have no choice but to endlessly google and try fumble something together)

Any help would be much appreciated!

Cheers,
Rachel
messages.body_snippet:
Hi there,

I have a dataset of approx 5000 loci for a suspected hybrid zone and 2 putative parent species. I've run the fixed difference function to determine the number of fixed loci between the two

messages.subject: Re: Generate reduced gl object with fixed differences only
messages.subject_clean: Generate reduced gl object with fixed differences only
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rachel,

The function gl.nhybrids does this for you. In a nutshell, the function

(a) Identifies loci that are fixed and different between the two sets of parental populations. You identify these with the p0 and p1 parameters. You can list more than one population each.
(b) Randomly samples 200 of the loci showing fixed differences, or if there are less than 200, takes them and selects additional loci base on information content (optionally).
(c) Outputs a genlight object with the final selection of 200 loci. You can use this to check that F1 hybrids are hets for all loci showing fixed differences (you should do this).
(d) Run the analysis several times to verify that the outcome is not sensitive to the random selection of loci.

The safest option is to run gl.nhybrids to produce the input file for New Hybrids and run it manually from there. Alternatively, you can give the script the directory containing the New Hybrids executable, set some parameters and let it rip from there. The output is a little more useful if you do it this way, but it is much more temperamental for some reason. Let me know if you have trouble.

Here is an example script you might find useful:

# ANALYSIS

      gl.stei.coll <- readRDS("Chelodina_stein_coll.Rdata")

    # New Hybrids Analysis

      # Set the parentals

        p0 <- c("ChsteSaltMillbi","ChsteYarrYarra")

        p1 <- "ChcolSwanPerth"

      # Run New Hybrids

        setwd("C:/workspace/R_analysis/R_chelodina")

        nhy <- gl.nhybrids(gl=gl.stei.coll, nhyb.directory = "C:/workspace/R/NewHybsPC", method="random", p0=p0, p1=p1, BurnIn = 10000, sweeps = 10000, outpath=getwd(), outfile="deleteme.txt")

      # Separate out the F1's and parentals for a check on error rate (F1 should be het for all loci, assuming no error rate on fixed differences -- but samples are small)

        nhy2 <- gl.keep.ind(nhy,c("MY04","MY05", "ATP501","ATP502", "UC_0238","UC_0227","UC_0228","UC_0230","UC_0231"),mono.rm=FALSE)

      # Convert to a matrix and invert

        tmat <- t(as.matrix(nhy2))

      # Tally homozygous ref, heterozygotes and homozygous alternate for the F1s (the homozygotes should be zero, theoretically)

        table(c(tmat[,"MY04"],tmat[,"MY05"]))

      # Calculate the false Error rate

      (table(c(tmat[,"MY04"],tmat[,"MY05"]))[1]+table(c(tmat[,"MY04"],tmat[,"MY05"]))[3])*100/ sum(table(c(tmat[,"MY04"],tmat[,"MY05"])))

        # There are 11 homozygotes ref and 1 homozygote alternate, total 12 = 4.7%, regarded within the acceptable error rate for fixed differences.

      # Output the scores

          write.csv(t(as.matrix(nhy2)),file="ch_stei_coll_loci.csv")

# ENDE
>
>

messages.subject: Re: dartR PCoA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yunjia,

Only so much we can do, as there are great plotting functions in R to draw upon and we try hard not to duplicate.

The gl.pcoa.plot function uses smart labels (that is, it attempts to ensure that the labels do not overlap with themselves or the points using package {directlabels\}), but this is a bit clunky, especially if there are many labels on the graph.

The easiest option is to export the graph as a vector graph (Export | Save as Image | Metafile) then edit it in a suitable graphics package (Adobe Illustrator, or I think Powerpoint can handle this). You can then drag the labels away from the points for clarity.

An alternative is to access the pcoa data directly. pcoa$scores (or whatever you called the pcoa object$scores) has the coordinates of the final solution, and you can then plot these with the full power of ggplot2.

If you are plotting so many labels because you want to identify the points, maybe explore using

gl.pcoa.plot( ......, labels="interactive", .......)
ggplotly()

You will need to make sure the package plotly is installed and loaded.

Then you can mouse over the points to identify them. If it is very crowded, you can select a region and zoom in.

Hope this helps.

messages.subject: Re: convert to bayescan input?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dale,

We do not have a conversion at the moment, but happy to write one. Not being familiar with the package, we would need some advice from you, as the manual is quite confusing.

Example file for SNPs is given in test_SNPs.txt. You have to indicate the number of loci and the number of populations before the actual genetic data (see the example). For each population, there is one line per locus numbered from 1 to the number of loci. Each lines has the same format as the following example:

8 24 2 4 10 0 6 3 1

“8” means that this is the 8th locus.
“24” is the total number of genes for this marker in this population (twice the number of individuals for diploid data). It can be different for different markers to account for missing data.
“2” is the number of alleles for the 8th locus. It has to be the same in all populations (even if some alleles are not observed in some populations).
“4 10 0 6 3 1” are the number of observations for each of the 2 alleles in this population for the 8th locus. These number must sum to the total number of genes in the population, here 24.

I assume from this that 4 10 is the count of the reference allele followed by the count of the alternate allele at each locus, but not sure. So there are pairs of values? Should not they be restricted to 0, 1 or 2 (or NA)? And would not the second count be redundant. Hence my confusion here.

Also, the example file has only two initial columns, not three (https://github.com/mfoll/BayeScan/blob/master/input_examples/test_genotype_SNP.txt)

Finally, I could not see where to code for missing data. There somewhere I am sure, but must have missed it.

Anyway, if you can sort this out for us, we can prepare and sent you a script, and then add it to the next release of dartR.

messages.subject: Re: not using 0 for average calculations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dale,

This is a question best put to DArT, but I think that AvgCountRef refers to the count of sequence tags that have the reference allele, averaged over all individuals. AvgCountSnp is similarly defined for the alternate allele. So if you add AvgCountRef and AvgCountSnp, you get a metric that is like the read depth for that locus. I have been unable to get a straight answer as to whether it is average read depth, or if not, what the difference is. Maybe you can sort this out in your discussions with DArT. Let me know.

We have added scripts to the next version gl.report.rdepth, gl.filter.rdepth that use these two metrics in their calculations.

Be aware that AvgCountRef and AvgCountSnp are calculated on the data from the service run, and are not adjusted when you take out individuals or populations. I might talk to DArT about how to work around this.

Arthur

messages.subject: Filtering by loci and individuals
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody!

I have a matrix of 71585 loci and 94 individuals divided into 6 populations. I need to filter my matrix but I am wondering if  there is some function that enable me do it in a way that the loci filtered are present in at least 50% of the individuals in each population.

Also, I am trying to understand the mathematics of the missing data. In my whole data (71585 loci), when I use the comand gl.report.callrate, it shows me that 1483 loci do not have missing data. Does it mean that those loci are present in all the 94 individuals? I am asking this because when I use the same comand for one of my populations, it shows that the population only have 996 loci and 330 among them have missing data. I am really confused.

I appreciate the support!
Kind regards,

Jessika

messages.subject: Re: Filtering by loci and individuals
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jessika,

You should use gl.report.callrate(gl, method="ind", plot=TRUE) to examine the call rate across individuals, then choose a threshold value to use in gl.filter.callrate(gl, method="ind", threshold=##). To answer your question, there is no quick way to select loci that are present in 50% of individuals apart from looking at the plot and tablulation by individual, and picking a suitable threshold.

Missing data is typically not "missing" in the sense that it was missed because of poor sequencing coverage, but "missing" because of a mutation at one or both of the restriction enzyme sites leading to fragment dropout. Missing data in the DArT dataset is more like null alleles.

So in your case, you have 71,585 loci of which 1,483 have been successfully scored across all individuals in your dataset. So you have it right.

Why then only 330 of 996 loci for one of your populations? I agree that is confusing. The most likely cause of this apparent discrepancy is that selecting only one population generates a number of monomorphic loci which are then removed (you can switch this off), and some of these would have been among the 1,483 with 100% call rate in the full dataset. So presumably, 1,153 of the 1,483 loci were monomorphic in the single population you are now considering. I would have to have a look at your data to confirm exactly what is going on.

I hope this helps. Please note the updated gl.report.callrate posted in response to a query earlier.

Hi Jessika,

Just following up on this. Your population assignments look fine, so no problem there. You can switch off filtering out monomorphs by setting the parameter mono.rm = FALSE when you run gl.filter.callrate.

Hope this helps.
